questions.prompt: Which layout minimizes memory traffic when a loop reads only the gz field of 2x10^5 IMU samples {t, ax, ay, az, gx, gy, gz}, each field a 4-byte float?
options: A std::map keyed by the index of each point
A linked list holding one node for each point
Structure of arrays (separate contiguous z array)
Array of structures (one whole struct per point)
questions.explanation: SoA streams only the needed field; AoS drags the other fields through the cache.

questions.prompt: A 2048x2048 row-major double matrix is summed column by column. Compared with row by row, what is expected?
options: Faster, because the columns are shorter than the rows
Identical speed, since both orders are O(n^2) in total work
Much slower, because every access touches a different cache line
Faster, because column sums vectorize better than row sums
questions.explanation: Stride of 16 KB between consecutive accesses wastes 7/8 of every loaded line and defeats prefetching.

questions.prompt: A time-versus-n plot on log-log axes is a straight line with slope about 1 for small n and bends upward at larger n. Most likely cause?
options: The compiler optimizations were switched off
The working set has outgrown a cache level
The algorithm switched to O(2^n) behavior
The timer overflowed at larger sizes
questions.explanation: Memory cost per element rises when data exceeds L1, L2, then L3.

questions.prompt: Which statement about perf record / perf report is correct?
options: It requires the program to be built with -fsanitize=address to give any output
It prints the exact asymptotic complexity of every function that it samples
It samples where the program spends time, so the top entries show where to look
It makes the program run faster by reordering its hottest functions in memory
questions.explanation: Sampling profilers attribute run time to functions; they need symbols (-g) for readable output.

questions.prompt: An array of 1000 doubles (8 bytes) is read with a stride of 8 elements (64 bytes). How many distinct 64-byte lines are touched? Integer.
questions.explanation: Elements 0, 8, ..., 992 = 125 reads, each in its own line: 125 lines (the sequential pass would touch 125 lines too).

questions.prompt: Timings: 1.5 s at n=1000, 6.0 s at n=2000, 24 s at n=4000. Estimate the exponent p of t ~ n^p. Give a number with 1 decimal.
questions.explanation: Each doubling multiplies time by 4, so p = 2.

questions.prompt: Profile: search 50%, serialization 30%, filter 20%. Search is made 10 times faster. Overall speedup? Give a number with 2 decimals.
Predict the time at n = 10000 for a routine fitted as t = 2e-6 * n^2 ms. Give a number in ms.
A colleague says: inserting in the middle of a std::list is O(1) and of a vector O(n), so lists are faster for our 5000-element queue. Evaluate the claim and propose how to settle it.
rubric: Big-O ignores constants and locality; at 5000 elements (tens of KB) the vector shift is a fast memmove inside cache.
Finding the insertion position in a list is O(n) pointer chasing, which dominates.
Settle with a benchmark at the real size and access pattern; mention median of repeated optimized runs.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Your node misses its 33 ms frame deadline occasionally. List the steps you would take, from measurement to change, and how you would verify the improvement.
rubric: Reproduce with a recorded input, measure with timers/perf in an optimized build, look at the distribution (tail) not only the mean.
Find the dominant contributor with a profiler; bound the gain with Amdahl's law before changing code.
Make one change, re-measure with the same method, keep a regression benchmark.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Write a function that estimates the exponent p from vectors of sizes and times by least squares on logs, and say what you check before trusting it.
rubric: Computes ln x and ln y, then slope = sum((lx-mx)(ly-my))/sum((lx-mx)^2).
Validates positive values, at least two distinct sizes (preferably four or more).
Checks the points are straight on a log-log plot and that no cache boundary is crossed in the fitted range.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: A data cache is 64 KiB, 8-way, with 64-byte lines. A column of a row-major matrix of doubles with 512 rows is read repeatedly. Which row width N (doubles) makes all 512 lines of the column fall in a single cache set?
questions.explanation: The cache has 65536/(8*64)=128 sets. Row r starts at byte 8Nr, so its set is floor(8Nr/64) mod 128. For N=2048 the row stride is 256 lines and 256 mod 128 = 0, so every row maps to the same set, which has only 8 ways: the column thrashes. N=2056 has stride 257 lines (step 1) and spreads over all 128 sets; N=2000 (250 lines, step 122, gcd 2) uses 64 sets; N=1536 (192 lines, step 64) uses 2 sets, which is bad but not a single set.

questions.prompt: Throughput model: DRAM latency L = 120 ns, peak bandwidth 12 bytes/ns, 64-byte lines, at most M = 8 cache-line fetches in flight. A program walks k = 6 independent shuffled linked lists in lock-step. Time per node in ns?
questions.explanation: Time per line = max(L/min(k,M), 64/bandwidth) = max(120/min(6,8), 64/12) = max(20, 5.33) = 20 ns. The loop is still latency bound: k=6 is below both M=8 and the saturation point L*bandwidth/64 = 22.5 lines.

questions.prompt: A routine is O(n) but timings at n = 2^8 ... 2^20 doubles give a fitted exponent of 1.3 over the whole range and 1.00 over the first four sizes, all inside L1. Explain the discrepancy and describe how you would design the size sweep and what you would report.
rubric: The cost per element is a step function of the working set (L1, L2, L3, DRAM), so the log-log curve is piecewise linear with bends; a single line fitted across bends gives an exponent above 1 even for an O(n) loop.
Fit only inside one regime (no cache boundary in the range, at least four sizes), and extrapolate only within that regime; the local exponent across a boundary can be 2 or more.
Sweep sizes on both sides of each cache capacity (from lscpu), report ns per element and the median of repeated optimized runs, and state the machine and the regime boundaries next to each slope.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
